newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo rates steady to firm in strong end.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo rates steady to firm in strong end.

text.p: Air cargo rates ex-UK remain generally steady to firmer with volumes at high levels in traditional year-end business, a Reuter survey shows.
Sterling's continued strength against other currencies does not so far seem to have had any major impact on British exports, industry sources added.

Although some carriers have cancelled flights over the holiday period, others are reporting flights leaving full on both Christmas and New Year's day. Handling problems at Heathrow are reportedly causing some delays, they said.
It is likely to be January before a clearer picture emerges and confirms the view, backed by some market players, that sterling's gains may be hitting exports.

In the meantime business is strong on all routes, especially to the Far East. Apart from each destination's own home market, a feature of recent weeks is the demand for space to China on direct and indirect flights.
This is being driven by mainland Chinese companies rushing to beat a year-end deadline for import tax changes on machinery, the sources added.

Rates to Narita are around an average of stg 2.10 a kg for 100 kgs compared to the previous stg 2.05, with Seoul also moving up to stg 2.05 from 2.00 stg. Hong Kong is close to an average of 1.25 a kg from 1.22 stg a kg for 100 kgs while Singapore is now at 1.30stg (1.29 stg).
Sydney has moved to 2.19 stg a kg --with some indirect routes at 1.60 stg - from 2.17 previously.

Japan Airlines Ltd is busy through to the New Year and "there's a very good possibility that it will the same afterwards, looking at the level of enquiries we've been having," said the carrier's Mike Mitchell.

At All Nippon Airlines,cargo manager John O'Shea said high passenger demand is having some impact on cargo capacity. But there is "no slowdown in demand and bookings are full for the seven days ahead."
"Within three to four weeks, we should have a better feel for how 1997 will turn out," he added.
Business at Korean Airlines Ltd "is going very well. We've also had enquiries for Hong Kong as firms are trying to meet the Chinese import deadline," said the carrier's cargo manager, Frank Smith.
Even apart from that deadline, there is a strong demand for space via Seoul to Chinese cities, including Beijing, Qingdao, Shenyang and Shanghai.
"And for the first time, we've had a request for space on our freighter to Shenzen airport, just across the border from Hong Kong," Smith added.

The London station was one of the few KAL stations in Europe: "to just about to meet its targets for 1996. We think next year will be pretty good and are looking at a 10 percent increase in revenue growth," he said.

Volumes to Korea itself remain at high levels. Marks and Spencer Ltd plans for franchise operations in the country have resulted in enquiries for the movement of nine main deck pallets a week, he added.
Cathay Pacific Cargo's James Gilliard said," it is still as crazy as ever. Business is really booming to Hong Kong. We expect to be fully booked over Christmas and just beyond."
"There's also good demand for Australia, although that is restricted by a lack of capacity out of Hong Kong."

Philippine Airlines, which operates non-stop Airbus A340s from London to Manila, is carrying a full 10 tonnes a flight, with a substantial amount destined for onward shipment to Australia, a airline source said.
"Order books suggest quite good business till at least mid-January and we're going out full on both Christmas and New Year's Day," he added.
The airline has not applied any cargo fuel surcharge and its existing rates will be held till the late spring review, he said.

Other industry sources confirmed the strength of demand to Australia with space at a premium on most carriers. And rates have remain firm despite the appearance of British charter carriers such as Air Tours and Britannia BRI.CN.
Malaysian Air System Bhd said December business was quieter than November, with a possible slowdown seen in January.
A cargo source said sterling's rise had had some impact on volumes and it was now targetting high-yield traffic. Demand for Australia and New Zealand is very good, they added.
The ex-UK market remains buoyant to most Far East and Australian destinations, said Singapore Airlines Ltd cargo manager, Barry Gibson.
He added that most airlines are trying to hold onto cargo yields and signs of weakness in the world's electronic industry may start to put yields under some pressure.

Looking at 1997, Gibson said it was difficult to anticipate trends,"but no one in their right minds would put up rates.' He said he was conservatively forecasting five percent volume growth next year with revenues up two to three percent.
To New York, the average per kg for 100 ks is unchanged at 0.63 stg, as is Chicago at 0.74 stg. However Chicago has gained two pence to 0.75 stg.

Virtually all of freight forwarder LEP International'a ex-UK global airfreight markets have performed "pretty well" during 1996, with the exception of the United States, said its director of product and carrier development Dermot Leeper.

"Our trans-Atlantic airfreight business has been a bit weak, particularly westbound, where following reduced demand, rates gradually fell during the year and are now lower than what they were at this time in 1995," he told Reuters.
Leeper added that he felt the strengthening of sterling would probably have a slightly adverse affect on demand for UK goods in the new year.

"UK exporters will be finding it a bit tougher to sell to the U.S. and other markets. But I don't see a drop in outbound air cargo from Britain -- just a smaller increase that we have become accustomed to. It won't be as much fun as before," he said.

British International Freight Association (BIFA) airfreight division manager Roger Blacklock described the UK-North American airfreight market as "a bit of a damp squib" this year compared to growth markets such as the Far East.
He gave over-capacity as part of the reason for this trend, but noted that business had gradually improved during the second half of the year.

Sharon Wright, UK group exports general manager of wholesaler Air Menzies International (AMI) said her company had seen a lot of growth in air cargo trade from Britain to North America, particularly in the last two to three months.
Lufthansa also said that while Britain-North America is not one of its main air cargo markets, business had definitely been on the rise over recent months.
"For the year as a whole on these routes, I would say that our ex-UK revenues are up by about five percent on 1995," said UK cargo marketing manager Rudiger Helm.
Continental Airlines' UK cargo sales manager Brian Coleman described his UK-U.S. business in the second half of 1996 as "fabulous".

"We have doubled our capacity and uplift to our main destinations of New York, Newark and Houston," he told Reuters. "We have been particularly pleased with excellent customer response to our 15 to 26-tonne capacity Manchester-New York DC-10 flights.
"These were introduced in September to take over from Boeing 757s, which can only carry two tonnes of cargo," he said.
He added that Continental had seen no ill effects on the carrier's ex-UK airfreight business resulting from the strengthening of the pound sterling.

"We are now in the traditional Christmas/new year slump period, which will continue through January. But once export production picks up again, I can see 1997 being just as busy for us in the UK as it has been this year. I see no signs of either an upturn or downturn," said Coleman.
Rates to Latin American have remained stable, with the average per kg to Sao Paulo up two pence at 2.08 and Buenos Aires down two pence to 2.23.

During 1997, Viking Freight Services -- a UK company contracted to sell cargo space on tour operator Unijet's ex-London Gatwick and Manchester charters to the U.S., flown by subsidiary Leisure International Airways -- said it has seen a sizeable growth in its business to Latin America during the year.

Viking managing director Kevin Durnin said that in order to diversify from the main long-haul route operated by Unijet, heavily congested UK-Florida, he had been trucking increasing amounts of cargo onward during the year to Miami to connect with Latin America-bound services.

"Through our deals with carriers such as Challenge, Fine Air, Tampa and Aeromexico, we have been doing well to Latin America and from Britain, that market is still buoyant...it is going really well," he said.
"In particular, there has been a continuing high demand for British consumer goods from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador and Brazil, in that order. And cargo rates have remained good," he added.

Lufthansa's Helm echoed Durnin's comments about the continuing strength of the UK-Latin America air cargo market, in which he said his carrier's revenues had increased by about five percent during 1996.

"We still find it difficult obtaining capacity on our flights out of Frankfurt to South America, especially when passenger aircraft are used. But I am very pleased with our cargo performance from the UK to Brazil in particular," he said.
Alitalia's outgoing northern Europe cargo manager Paul Rodwell said he was also currently finding it difficult to obtain space for UK-originating freight on his carrier's Latin America-bound flights.

"Priority is usually given to Italy-originating traffic, which makes things difficult and harder for us to compete in Britain with other carriers to Latin America," said Rodwell, who will next month be joining handling company, the London Cargo Group.

"For Alitalia, the UK is considered as a top-up market for Latin America. But we have improved our yields here, even if at present it is even harder to get space because of the usual seasonal rise in passengers and their baggage to the detriment of the cargo payload," he said.
BIFA's Blacklock noted that in general, airfreight business from Britain to Latin America was weak in the first half of this year but had picked up over the past two to three months.
Rates to the Middle East -- Dubai and Bahrain -- are also steady at average of 0.87 stg a kg for 100 kgs to Dubai and 0.95 stg to Bahrain.
Cargo traffic is at or close to capacity levels to the Middle East, with substantial volumes also destined for the Far East and Australia.
"We are extremely busy till after Christmas," said a cargo executive from Emirates ,while Royal Jordanian's Fawal Qarden said the carrier was "operating at full capacity."

Some 70 percent of the Amman-based airline's cargo ex-UK is for transhipment to the Far East. It is operating daily A310s as well as twice weeky Boeing 707 freighters from Gatwick. The airline is introducing a cargo fuel surcharge from January 1.
He added that so far " sterling's strength has had no visible impact. Business is holding up well."

Emirates with twice daily Boeing 777s from Heathrow and an Airbus 310 or 300 from Manchester - via Zurich - is carying some 45 to 50 tonnes. "Demand is strong. We've got lots of agents looking for space," the executive said.
Sterling's strength has had no impact, "but then the market is traditionally strong at this time of the year".

On routes into Europe, there is still some impact from the Channel Tunnel fire and the French truckers' strike. These produce a severe distortion in traffic patterns at the time and it is not yet clear that the distortions have been completely removed, industry sources.

There was some firming in European rates but perhaps more important in the longer-term is the view by some industry experts that major logistics users -- for example, car producers -- will at the very least closely review their contingency distribution plans.
And that "could well mean greater and faster use of airfreight to overcome transport bottlenecks," they added.

Traffic to South Africa has held up better than expected earlier in the year. Despite competition from both direct and indirect carriers, rates are still around the 1.80 stg per kg for 100 kg , but much lower prices are available.

David Hall for Air Gabon - which started a weekly 747 combi service via Libreville this year - said they moving some 28 tonnes a week ex-UK, compared to forecasts of 20 tonnes. This also includes six tonnes for Libreville.
Like some other airlines, Air Gabon has not introduced a fuel surcharge but an increase in rates is expected in the New Year. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
